rows.label: Concept
rows.text: This chapter separates formal from informal letters and gives the part-by-part order of each. A formal letter runs sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, closing (Yours faithfully) and signature, while an informal letter runs date, salutation (Dear Name), opening, body, closing (Love or Yours) and signature.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
A formal letter closes with 'Yours faithfully' and carries a signature, while an informal letter closes with 'Love' or 'Yours'.
Use 'Dear Sir/Madam' when the name of the receiver is unknown.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Formal letters need 'Dear Sir' without name. ✅ Use 'Dear Sir/Madam' if name unknown.  ·  ❌ Emails are informal. ✅ Professional emails require formal tone.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Formal letters need 'Dear Sir/Madam' when no name is known, not a bare 'Dear Sir' with a missing name.  ·  Emails are not automatically informal; a professional email requires a formal tone.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Write a formal letter to the editor complaining about poor road conditions.  ·  Write an application for a scholarship to the principal.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Never leave out the subject line of a formal letter - it is among the first things an examiner checks.  ·  In a complaint or editor's letter, state the problem first, then the cause, then a suggested remedy, then a courteous request.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Write a formal letter to the editor about pollution in Kathmandu.  ·  Write an inquiry letter asking for information.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Parts memory hook for a formal letter: 'Send Date Receive Subject Salute Body Close Sign'.  ·  Layout shortcut: block style puts every part flush left on a new line; semi-block style indents the body paragraphs within the same arrangement.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Write an inquiry letter asking for details about a course.  ·  Write an email to a friend about your summer vacation plans.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Format carries marks: address, date, subject, salutation, body, closing and signature must appear in the correct order.  ·  MCQ traps: treating emails as informal, and writing 'Dear Sir/Madam' when a name has been given.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Formal letter format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body, closing and signature  ·  Informal letter format: date, salutation, opening, body, closing and signature  ·  Formal letter types: application, complaint, inquiry and editor's letter  ·  Informal letter types: friendly letter, thank-you letter and congratulatory letter

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Formal order: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, closing (Yours faithfully), signature.  ·  Informal order: date, salutation (Dear Name), opening, body, closing (Love or Yours), signature.  ·  Formal types: application for jobs, admissions and leaves; complaint; inquiry; and editor's letter expressing opinion on a public issue.  ·  Informal types: friendly letter for catching up, thank-you letter for gratitude, and congratulatory letter for celebrating achievements.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Write a thank-you letter to a friend who helped you during an illness.

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Keep the tone consistent from the salutation to the closing - formal letters stay formal, informal letters stay warm and conversational.  ·  Block style is the safest layout in the exam because it is the hardest to mark incorrectly.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: In a formal letter, the subject line is written: → C  ·  If the name of the receiver is unknown, the correct salutation is: → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 1. Formal Letter Format  ·  Sender's address → Date → Receiver's address → Subject → Salutation (Sir/Madam) → Body → Closing (Yours faithfully) → Signature  ·  ### 2. Informal Letter Format

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Salutation rules: 'Dear Sir/Madam' when the name is unknown, 'Dear Name' for a known person  ·  Standard layouts: block style with every part on a new line, and semi-block style with indented body paragraphs  ·  Email writing: a clear concise subject line, a formal tone for professional mail, and short paragraphs.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Exam tasks: a formal letter to the editor about pollution in Kathmandu, and an application for a scholarship.  ·  In an application, give your qualifications and the reason for applying before you make the request, and keep one clear request per letter.  ·  A formal letter requires a subject line, placed between the receiver's address and the salutation.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Professional emails require a formal tone even though email is a digital medium.  ·  An email subject line must be clear and concise, and its paragraphs should be kept short.  ·  Applications are used for jobs, admissions and leaves; inquiry letters ask for information; complaint letters concern products, services or conditions.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: If the receiver is named, such as the principal, write 'Dear Sir'; if the name is unknown, write 'Dear Sir/Madam'.  ·  Time-saving formula for an editor's letter: problem, cause, suggestion, request - one paragraph each.  ·  For an informal letter, open warmly and close with 'Love' or 'Yours'; 'Yours faithfully' belongs to formal letters only.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: This chapter is about format, type and tone; do not add grammar rules that are not in these notes.  ·  Date → Salutation (Dear Name) → Opening → Body → Closing (Love/Yours) → Signature  ·  ### 3. Formal Letter Types
